title: Four kinds of samana
hookLine: Cunda the smith asks how many kinds of wandering seekers there are
last: PLANT ONE SEED YOU CAN'T SEE.

lines: HOW DO YOU TELL THEM APART?
cards: A news story breaks about a religious leader who did something terrible, and at the dinner table someone says: see, they're all the same. It's an old sentence, and a sharp one.
The fifth poem of the Sutta Nipata takes it on. A metalworker named Cunda, the smith's son, asks the Buddha: how many kinds of samanas are there in the world?
A samana is a wandering seeker, someone who has left home for the spiritual life. Cunda wants to know how to tell them apart.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO HAS CONQUERED THE PATH
teach.b: The Buddha answers: four, and no fifth. The first has conquered the path: beyond doubt, free of the arrow, delighting in freedom, a guide for the world.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO SHOWS IT, THE ONE WHO LIVES IT
teach.b: The second shows the path: knows the highest as the highest, explains it and lays it out right here, cutting through other people's doubts.
The third lives the path: well restrained, mindful, walking the well-taught way, doing no harm.
The fourth defiles the path. He wears the same robe as the good ones and looks the part.

teach.h: ONE FRAUD DOESN'T MAKE THEM ALL
teach.b: But he's pushy, deceitful, unrestrained, a fraud in disguise, and he spoils the families who trust him. The poem calls him chaff. Then comes the answer to the dinner table.

A lay follower who has heard and understood this sees the fourth kind for what he is, and doesn't lose trust in the others because of him. How could the pure and the impure be the same? Notice the order.
Tradition reads the first as the Buddha himself.
But the second, the one who shows, is any good teacher who explains clearly and clears up doubt. You don't have to have arrived to point the way well.
And the warning in the fourth is honest: the robe alone proves nothing. A poem that names its own frauds this plainly is taking trust seriously.

how: In Buddhist communities the monastic code sets standards for those who wear the robe, and lay supporters help hold monastics to them; Cunda's poem is one text Buddhists turn to on telling sincere seekers from pretenders.

o: a village priest who leads sacrifices
a lay follower who supports monks
a wandering seeker who has left home

games.q: four kinds of samana: tap the pairs.
p: beyond doubt, a guide for the world
explains the way and clears up doubts
wears the robe, a fraud in disguise

s: the poem says there are four kinds of samana, and no fifth
conqueror, shower, liver and defiler of the path.
the poem says you can always spot a fraud by his robe
the defiler wears the same robe as the good ones; the robe alone proves nothing.
the poem says one fraud should make you distrust them all
a follower who understands doesn't lose trust in the good because of the bad.

games.q: you're a lay follower. you've just learned that one robed monk in your town is a fraud. what does Cunda's poem say you'll do?
o: see him for what he is and keep trust in the good ones.
games.why: the poem's last verses: the wise follower isn't misled, for how could the pure and impure be the same?

practice: Remember someone who showed you a good path, a teacher, a coach, a grandparent, a friend who explained something kindly: not someone who had it all figured out, just someone who pointed clearly.
See their face and thank them silently, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: samana. Cunda's question: the one who conquers the path, the one who shows it, the one who lives it, and the one who wears the robe and defiles it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samana (Sanskrit shramana): a wandering seeker who has left home, of any school in the Buddha's India.

carryVoice: Your line: the one who shows. One fraud doesn't make them all the same. Until tomorrow.
